# Using BrowserDo

BrowserDo's `browser_*` tools drive Embiody, a browser on the person's Windows computer. The
person may be using the same browser at the same time. When these tools are available, use them for
every web task, even a quick search for news or a fact, rather than a built-in web search, a fetch
tool or another browser, unless the person asks for one. If the tools are deferred (only their
names are listed), load the ones you need in one tool search first, for example
`browser_read_pages`, `browser_new_tab`, `browser_input_text` and `browser_take_snapshot`.

## Read and search

- To read pages, pass their URLs to `browser_read_pages`, several at once. Use it instead of
  WebFetch or a built-in search tool: it returns the page's own text, including pages built by
  scripts and sites the person is signed in to.
- To search, open the search engine's (or the site's) home page with `browser_new_tab` and type
  the query into its search box with `browser_input_text` and `pressEnter`. Opening a results
  URL directly often meets a captcha. Then snapshot the results with `showLinks` and pass the
  result addresses (not ads) to `browser_read_pages`.

## Act on a page

1. `browser_take_snapshot` first. It lists the page's elements, each actionable one with a
   number, and returns a `snapshotId`.
2. Act by element number together with that `snapshotId`. Never guess a number or reuse one from
   an older snapshot.
3. Prefer `browser_batch`, even for a single action: it runs clicks, typing and key presses in a
   row and returns a fresh snapshot, so you need fewer calls.
4. Snapshot again before acting on something an earlier step made appear.

Ask for `includeImage` when the look matters, such as which option is selected or a chart.

## Leave some things to the person

Sign-in, captchas and payment are for the person; never solve a captcha or type a password
yourself. Hand the tab over with `browser_start_human_control`, snapshot until they are done,
then call `browser_stop_human_control`. If no one is there to answer, stop and say what is needed.

## Work in your own tabs

Open tabs with `browser_new_tab` and pass their `tabId` to every call that acts on a tab. Leave
the person's own tabs alone unless asked.

## First run

The first time BrowserDo starts, it downloads and installs the Embiody browser, which takes a few
minutes. Until then each tool replies with the progress; call `browser_status` or `browser_wait`
and try again.

# BrowserDo

Website: [embiody.com/browserdo](https://embiody.com/browserdo/)

[![Listed on mcpservers.org](https://mcpservers.org/badge.svg)](https://mcpservers.org/servers/zhaijunlong/browserdo)

[![BrowserDo demo: the agent fills 4 form fields in 2.5 seconds, shops in its own tabs, keeps going while minimized, fills a checkout in one combo and hands you the tab to pay](assets/browserdo-demo.gif)](https://youtu.be/hIqfkx8bA98)

**Built for AI agents. Shared with people.**

[Embiody](https://embiody.com) is a Windows browser your AI agent works in, in the background and
at full speed, while you keep using your PC and can step in at any time. BrowserDo is the
[MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that connects your agent to it. Add it to Claude
Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, VS Code or Gemini CLI, and your agent can browse, click, type
and read pages, including sites you are signed in to.

## Why BrowserDo

Each point below has a short clip recorded on real sites. The side-by-side ones run the same task
at the same moment through Playwright MCP and BrowserDo, from one Claude Code session.

### 1. Works in the background at full speed, and leaves your screen to you

[![Chrome and Embiody countdowns in a background tab, behind a window and minimized](assets/readme/point-01.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-01.mp4)
*Chrome and Embiody countdowns in a background tab, behind a window and minimized. Click for the 38-second clip.*

Pages run at full speed in background tabs, background windows, minimized windows and hidden
windows. Your agent does not need the browser in front of you, so you keep using your computer
while it works, and it can work in a dozen tabs at once.

Ordinary Chrome slows down pages you are not looking at. In our test, a browser window was
completely covered by another window for 7 minutes:

| | Timers | A countdown on the page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Embiody, front tab | 10 per second throughout | on time |
| Embiody, background tab | 10 per second throughout | on time |
| Chrome, front tab | slowed down after 12 seconds | 355 seconds behind |

No launch flags are needed for this. One limit: a page opened *while* its window is minimized
may come back without a screenshot; its text and element numbers are still there.

### 2. Works where bots get blocked — because it isn't one

[![Walmart, Target, adidas and realtor.com stop Playwright MCP with a bot check; Embiody goes straight through](assets/readme/point-02.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-02.mp4)
*Walmart, Target, adidas and realtor.com stop Playwright MCP with a bot check; Embiody goes straight through. Click for the 24-second clip.*

Your agent works in your own browser, on your behalf, so sites with anti-bot protection treat it
the way they treat you. We also signed in to an account on a site protected by a leading
commercial bot-detection service, the kind that usually stops automation tools.

### 3. Sees the whole page and clicks the right thing

[![On nytimes.com a privacy overlay swallows Playwright MCP’s click; BrowserDo gives the agent only the overlay’s buttons, so it closes it first](assets/readme/point-03.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-03.mp4)
*On nytimes.com a privacy overlay swallows Playwright MCP’s click; BrowserDo gives the agent only the overlay’s buttons, so it closes it first. Click for the 28-second clip.*

- Elements covered by a popup or overlay get no number, so the agent can't click something you
  can't see.
- Content inside embedded frames from other sites, such as payment forms and sign-in boxes, can
  be read and clicked.
- Long pages are read whole, not only the part on screen.
- An element off screen is scrolled into view before it is clicked.
- Clicks land where they should across multiple monitors and at any display scaling.
- Every element number belongs to one snapshot. A number from an older snapshot is refused
  before anything is clicked, instead of hitting whatever took its place.

### 4. You can see what the agent is doing

[![The "AI-controlled tab" badge, then the highlighted border and the agent’s own cursor](assets/readme/point-04.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-04.mp4)
*The "AI-controlled tab" badge, then the highlighted border and the agent’s own cursor. Click for the 15-second clip.*

A tab the agent is working in shows a virtual mouse pointer, a frame around the page and a
marker on the tab. Open it any time to watch.

### 5. You and the agent share one tab

[![Disputing a charge on Uber Help: the agent hands you the tab for the sign-in code, then takes it back](assets/readme/point-05.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-05.mp4)
*Disputing a charge on Uber Help: the agent hands you the tab for the sign-in code, then takes it back. Click for the 38-second clip.*

The agent fills in the forms; you step in for the sign-in code, the captcha or the payment, then
hand the tab back, and the agent picks up where you left off. If you click or type in a tab the
agent is working in, you are asked whether to take it over. The agent asks before it touches a
tab of yours.

### 6. Fewer tokens for the whole page

[![Tokens per whole-page snapshot: Playwright MCP, Chrome DevTools MCP and BrowserDo on Wikipedia, GitHub, CNN, ESPN and Apple](assets/readme/point-06-tokens.jpg)](assets/readme/point-06-tokens.jpg)

The browser engine itself boils each page down for the agent: its text, plus every element the
agent can act on, numbered. On Wikipedia, GitHub, CNN, ESPN and Apple, a whole-page snapshot took
37% of the tokens of Playwright MCP's (o200k tokenizer, same 1600×1000 viewport, November 2026),
and the agent can read just the screen it is working on.

### 7. Several steps in one call

[![Real speed: the agent fills 4 form fields in 2.5 seconds with one call](assets/readme/point-07.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-07.mp4)
*Real speed: the agent fills 4 form fields in 2.5 seconds with one call. Click for the 3-second clip.*

`browser_batch` runs several actions (clicks, typing, key presses) in a row and returns a fresh
snapshot of the page, so the agent needs fewer round trips and fewer tokens.

### 8. Reads the page itself, not a summary

[![A JB Hi-Fi search page: Claude Code’s built-in fetch gets a browser warning and 0 products; BrowserDo reads all 18 with prices](assets/readme/point-08.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-08.mp4)
*A JB Hi-Fi search page: Claude Code’s built-in fetch gets a browser warning and 0 products; BrowserDo reads all 18 with prices. Click for the 30-second clip.*

`browser_read_pages` returns the page's own text, links included, from pages built by scripts and
from sites you are signed in to. It can stand in for Claude Code's WebFetch, which fetches the page
without running its scripts and hands back a short model-written summary.

### 9. Sees the browser's own popups

[![McDonald’s store finder asks for your location: Playwright MCP’s agent never sees the prompt; BrowserDo reports it and the agent allows it once](assets/readme/point-09.gif)](https://embiody.com/assets/video/points/point-09.mp4)
*McDonald’s store finder asks for your location: Playwright MCP’s agent never sees the prompt; BrowserDo reports it and the agent allows it once. Click for the 30-second clip.*

Permission bubbles, menus, Save As dialogs, "Leave site?" prompts and alerts are reported in every
snapshot, with the ways each one can be answered.

### 10. Current engine, signed releases

Built on Chromium 156. The installer carries the digital signature of SELECTIOUS PTY LTD, which
BrowserDo verifies before running it, and the browser updates itself, checking the signature of
every update.

## Requirements

- Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit (Embiody is Windows only for now)
- Node.js 20 or newer. Check with `node -v`. Without it, BrowserDo fails to start (Claude Code shows
  "Failed to connect"). Install it with `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS`, then restart your client.
- The Embiody browser, version 0.9.0.3 or newer: installed automatically the first time BrowserDo
  starts. That is a download of about 140 MB and takes a few minutes; your client can use BrowserDo
  at once, and until the browser is ready each tool replies with the progress. With an older one, BrowserDo opens the browser's update page and asks you to restart
  the browser and BrowserDo once it has updated ([details](docs/browser-versions.md)).

No API key is needed. Your agent drives the browser with its own model.

## Install

BrowserDo runs as `npx -y browserdo-mcp`. Pick your client and follow only that section; the others
are for other clients.

### Claude Code

```bash
claude mcp add browserdo -- npx -y browserdo-mcp
```

Add `--scope project` to share it with your team through `.mcp.json`, or `--scope user` to use it
in every project.

### Claude Desktop

Edit `%APPDATA%\Claude\claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserdo": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Codex

```bash
codex mcp add browserdo -- npx -y browserdo-mcp
```

Or add to `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.browserdo]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
```

### Cursor

Add to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` (all projects) or `.cursor/mcp.json` (one project):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserdo": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code

Run **MCP: Add Server** from the Command Palette, choose **Command (stdio)** and enter
`npx -y browserdo-mcp`. Or add to `.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "browserdo": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Gemini CLI

Add to `~/.gemini/settings.json` (all projects) or `.gemini/settings.json` (one project):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserdo": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

### Other MCP clients

Add a local (stdio) MCP server in your client's settings, with command `npx` and arguments
`-y browserdo-mcp`. Most clients take it in this shape:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "browserdo": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Then ask your agent to do something on the web:

> Find me a direct flight from Sydney to Melbourne next Wednesday morning and show me the
> three cheapest options.

## Tools

Each tool is one browser action. `windowId` and `tabId` are optional everywhere; leave them out
and the frontmost window and tab are used.

| Tool | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `browser_take_snapshot` | The page as one line per element, each actionable element with a number, plus the page position, URL, title, any popups in the way and a `snapshotId`. Says when the page is a PDF, an error page or a crashed tab. `includeImage` adds the annotated screenshot; `readWholePage` reads beyond the screen. |
| `browser_read_pages` | Read up to 10 pages at once in background tabs and get their text, with links as footnotes. |
| `browser_batch` | Several actions on one tab in a row, then a fresh snapshot. Stops at the first failure, and after a step that changed the page. |
| `browser_click`, `browser_input_text`, `browser_press_key`, `browser_select_editable_text`, `browser_scroll` | Act on an element by its number and the `snapshotId` it came from. `browser_input_text` can also edit at a place named by the surrounding words. |
| `browser_move`, `browser_drag` | Hover; press, carry and release. Drag works sliders, canvases and reorderable lists. |
| `browser_navigate`, `browser_go_back`, `browser_go_forward`, `browser_reload`, `browser_stop_loading`, `browser_wait` | Getting around. |
| `browser_get_window_info`, `browser_new_window`, `browser_close_window`, `browser_show`, `browser_minimize` | Windows. `browser_get_window_info` lists every window and tab with their ids. |
| `browser_new_tab`, `browser_select_tab`, `browser_close_tab`, `browser_set_audio_muted` | Tabs. |
| `browser_close_popup_bubble` | Answer a permission bubble or dialog. |
| `browser_start_human_control`, `browser_stop_human_control` | Hand the tab to a person for a password or captcha, then take it back. |
| `browser_status` | Whether the browser is ready, or how far its first install has got. |

## Settings

Set these in the `env` block of your client's config, or put them in a config file (copy
`browserdo.config.example.yaml` to `browserdo.config.yaml` next to where the server runs, or pass
`--config <path>`). Environment variables win over the config file.

| Variable | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `EMBIODY_TOOLS` | `browser` (the tools above), `task` (`browser_run_task` only) or `all` (default). |
| `EMBIODY_SAVE_SNAPSHOTS` | `1` saves every snapshot's screenshots and page text under `run/browser_data`, for debugging. Off by default. |
| `EMBIODY_EXE_PATH` | Launch your own Embiody build, on a separate profile, instead of the installed one. |
| `EMBIODY_USER_DATA_DIR` | Give the agent a separate profile folder instead of your own Embiody; BrowserDo then starts a browser of its own on it. |
| `EMBIODY_VLLM_ENDPOINT`, `EMBIODY_VLLM_MODEL`, `EMBIODY_VLLM_API_KEY` | The model for `browser_run_task` (below). |

The example config file explains the rest: fallback models, timeouts, how long to let pages
settle. `--transport sse` serves MCP over HTTP at `http://127.0.0.1:3000/sse` instead of stdio; it
answers this machine only.

## Privacy

BrowserDo has no telemetry, usage statistics or error reporting.

- **Downloads**: the first time it starts without Embiody installed, it downloads the installer
  from GitHub, or from a mirror if GitHub can't be reached. The installer carries the digital
  signature of SELECTIOUS PTY LTD; BrowserDo checks it before running the installer and refuses
  one that is unsigned or signed by anyone else.
- **Updates**: when your client starts BrowserDo with `npx`, npm checks the npm registry for the
  latest version when it starts BrowserDo. That request is made by npm, not by BrowserDo.
- **Your model**: only `browser_run_task` sends anything to a model, and only to the endpoint you
  configure. The browser tools return pages to your own agent.
- **On your computer**: a debug log at `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Embiody\BrowserDo\logs` records the URLs
  visited and the steps taken, never page content or your task. It keeps at most three 5 MB files.
  Snapshots are not saved unless you set `EMBIODY_SAVE_SNAPSHOTS=1`.
- **Your profile**: the agent works in your own Embiody, in its Default profile, so it can use
  the sites you are signed in to there. Other Embiody profiles are not used, and neither are other
  browsers on your computer, such as Chrome or Edge. To keep the agent
  apart, set `EMBIODY_USER_DATA_DIR` to a folder of its own.

See the [privacy policy](https://embiody.com/privacy) and the
[Embiody end-user license agreement](https://embiody.com/eula).

## Optional: `browser_run_task`

If you would rather hand over a whole task than drive the browser step by step,
`browser_run_task` runs it inside BrowserDo with a vision model of your choice (any
OpenAI-compatible endpoint), and keeps the screenshots out of your agent's context.

```json
"env": {
  "EMBIODY_VLLM_ENDPOINT": "<your-openai-compatible-endpoint>",
  "EMBIODY_VLLM_MODEL": "<your-vision-model>",
  "EMBIODY_VLLM_API_KEY": "<your-api-key>"
}
```

| Parameter | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `task` | **Required.** The task, in plain language. |
| `windowId`, `tabId` | Pass both to continue an earlier task in the same tab. |
| `maxRounds` | Default 12. |
| `closeTabWhenDone`, `closeBrowserWindowWhenDone` | Default false. |
| `humanReply` | Your answer to the question a previous run stopped on, when your client can't ask you mid-task. |

When the task needs you, it asks. A step only you can do, like a password or a code sent to you,
hands you the tab first and continues once you say you're done. In clients that support
questions during a task (`tasks.requests.elicitation.create`, as in Claude Code), the question
appears in your conversation; elsewhere the task ends with the question, and you answer by calling
it again with `humanReply`.

`browser_stop_task` stops a running task at the end of its current step.

**Keep your API key out of files that get committed.** If your client can expand environment
variables in its config, use that; otherwise keep the key in a config file outside the repository
and point at it with `--config`.

## Notes

- **Claude Code keeps old tool definitions in a conversation.** After BrowserDo is upgraded, start
  a new conversation to see new tools and parameters.
- BrowserDo speaks MCP protocol version `2025-11-25` and negotiates down to older versions.

## Development

```bash
npm install
npm run build
npm test          # 902 tests
npm run test:fast # unit and module tests only
```

See `test/README.md` for the test layout.

# Tests

Node's own `node --test`, with no extra test framework. TypeScript is compiled to `.test-out/`
by `tsconfig.test.json` first, and the compiled output is what runs.

```bash
npm test              # unit + module + integration + contract (634 tests, ~8s)
npm run test:fast     # unit + module (541 tests, ~0.6s — the loop to run while editing code)
npm run test:unit
npm run test:module
npm run test:integration
npm run test:contract
npm run test:live     # a real browser; needs a build, see below
```

`npm test` and `npm run test:fast` run `npm run check:comments` first. It catches a `/**` that
lost its closing `*/`, which swallows the code beneath it — something `tsc` does not report when
what vanished is only used by the tests or the scripts.

## The layers

Layers are separated by **what outside thing each one needs**, not by how deep it tests —
because that is what decides where and how often it can run.

| Layer | Directory | Under test | Where the stand-ins are | Needs | Tests | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **unit** | `unit/` | Pure functions, pure data transforms | None | Nothing | 270 | 0.23s |
| **module** | `module/` | One module | Its only outside collaborator (CDP) | The corpus group needs `run/corpus`; skipped without it | 271 | 0.27s |
| **integration** | `integration/` | Several real modules assembled together | Only at process boundaries (a CDP stand-in plus a local fake-model HTTP server) | One local port | 77 | 7.0s |
| **contract** | `contract/` | The protocol we agreed with the browser kernel | A CDP stand-in, but checked against the real `embiody_protocol.pdl` | An embiody checkout | 16 | 0.20s |
| **live** | `live/` | The whole chain | None | A real browser build | 21 | 12s |

The first three are the usual pyramid. The last two are **orthogonal boundary guards**: they do
not test our own logic, they test whether our agreement with the thing outside still holds —
contract guards the kernel protocol, live guards the real browser.

### What puts a test in each layer

- **unit**: it still runs with every stand-in removed. Data in, data out.
- **module**: the subject is the behaviour of **one** module; even where it calls into other real
  modules, the assertion is about this module's own job. The test is "whose behaviour is this
  assertion describing".
- **integration**: the assertion is about **orchestration across modules** — what runs first, how
  state is passed, how one module's output becomes another's input. No single module can be
  looked at to see it.
- **contract**: the thing being asserted about **is not in this repository**.
- **live**: real process, real I/O.

`module/runtime-executor.test.ts` is a borderline case: it really does call into
`browser-actions`, but the assertions are about the executor's routing and argument mapping, so
it is a module test. Such cases are decided by "whose behaviour is being described"; there is no
harder line, and no point pretending there is.

## What each file tests

### unit/

| File | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `runtime-plan.test.ts` | `normalizeRuntimePlan`: merging synonymous statuses, hard field constraints, the block list (11 deleted or renamed commands). Those commands used to report success unconditionally, so the model's old habits have to be stopped. |
| `prompt-consistency.test.ts` | The prompt given to the model matches the real action table: no action missing or extra, the actions in the examples exist, output-contract field names line up with the Zod schema, retired names are gone. This chain breaks easily and breaks silently — add an action and forget the prompt, and the code is green, the tests are green, and the model never learns the action exists. |
| `action-batch.test.ts` | The contract for several actions in one round: `action_calls` has exactly one shape, an array (a bare object and the old `action_call` name are normalised); one illegal action rejects the whole batch; `isBatchTerminatingAction` covers every action in the table (a new action has to declare itself); the cap comes from the config. |
| `read-coverage.test.ts` | Which parts of a page the model has seen, per scrolling area: ranges merge, gaps are named, and above all **an area whose text no longer agrees where two rounds overlap starts over** (a filtered list or an opened mail in the same pane must not inherit coverage it never earned), while a few changed lines (ads, countdowns) do not reset it and a sticky pane that moved stays one area. |
| `launch-config.test.ts` | `buildLaunchArgs()` contains no flag from Chrome's `kBadFlags`; `extraFlags` appends rather than replaces; the profile is derived from the exe path. Both failures are easy to miss: an infobar pushes the viewport down so coordinates no longer line up, and a shared profile means the custom build never launched at all. |

### module/

| File | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `browser-actions.test.ts` | Each action's payload and how its reply is read: the six `loadStatus` values, required-argument checks (15 actions), `formResubmission`, exhausted history entries, what `wasLoading` / `muted` mean, snapshot field names, input focus retry, `browserScroll`'s parameters as renamed in late September 2026 (the retired `yDistance` never on the wire, `toY: 0` kept), emsn and coordinates being mutually exclusive, and the three ways a drag may name its destination. Reading any of these wrongly raises no error — it just hands the model a success that is not one. |
| `runtime-executor.test.ts` | Routing for 19 actions; `windowId` / `tabId` come only from the runtime's working target (whatever the model fills in is ignored — it has no real ids); the `waitUntil` allow-list; `targetUpdate` / `landedUrl`. |
| `observe-plan.test.ts` | Working out which tabs to capture: the model names them, this round's layout validates them, the list is settled. An invented tabId, a closed tab, more than 20 at once, the same tab twice — all handled before the kernel is called, and **reported back to the model**. Plus `snapshotBlockedReason`: a blank page and a tab that is neither an agent tab nor in the foreground must not be sent for capture at all — the latter makes the kernel **wait forever**. |
| `discover-target.test.ts` | Target selection order, agent tab → blank page → first; parsing a `TabInfo` object; empty and malformed shapes. Blindly taking `windows[0].tabs[0]` steals the tab a person is using. |
| `annotated-content-corpus.test.ts` | The renderer run against **real page snapshots**: no text, number, name, value or placeholder may be lost, bboxes are complete, and the size saving is real. Hand-written little trees cannot cover the shapes real pages have — the first renderer passed every unit test and still lost text on 182 of 1195 real snapshots. The corpus is read from `run/corpus` (`EMBIODY_CORPUS_DIR` overrides it); the directory is not in the repository, and the whole group is skipped without it. |

### integration/

| File | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `runtime-loop.test.ts` | The whole main loop: bootstrap order, the landed url, tab state fed into the prompt, handing a sensitive step to a person, taking control back on resume, the person refusing to hand it back, a failed action not being fatal, the cleanup switches. Human takeover is a state machine spanning several rounds, and only an end-to-end run reaches it — it caught a real bug on the spot: when the model called `browserStartHumanControl` itself, the handover ran twice. |

### contract/

| File | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `protocol-contract.test.ts` | **The most important group here.** Every action is actually run (against a fake CDP), the command name and payload keys it emits are recorded, and each is checked against `embiody_protocol.pdl`: does the command exist, is every key sent a declared parameter, is every non-optional parameter actually sent, do the reply fields we read exist, do `TabInfo` / `WindowInfo` fields agree, does the navigation reply really have no `success`, is `waitUntil` mixed up with `loadStatus`. The browser's earlier round of breaking protocol changes (`browserGetWindowInfos` becoming singular, tabs becoming an array of objects) should all have been caught here. |

Two deliberate choices in how it is written:

- **The pdl content is not copied into the test**; the test reads the real file. Copy it and the
  test stays green after the protocol changes, which defeats the point.
- **Payload keys are recorded by really running each action**, not by scanning the source with a
  regex. Scanning misses payloads assembled at runtime — `browserScroll` deciding by value
  whether to send `deltaX` is exactly that.

### live/

| File | What it tests |
|---|---|
| `live-browser.test.ts` | Concurrent capture across tabs (a background tab yields an image, does not steal the foreground, does not fall back to waiting for paint), a background tab that is not an agent tab really hanging rather than erroring, protocol probing, `TabInfo` fields all present, a new background agent tab, `canGoBack` agreeing with actually going back, mute reading back, `annotatedContent` really arriving, reads working and writes not during human takeover, retired commands really failing hard. |

A fake CDP can only show that *we send what was agreed*; a real browser shows that *the kernel
answers as agreed*. Both are needed.

## Running the live tests

They are not part of `npm test`. `npm run test:live` runs them, and they must be switched on
explicitly:

```bash
# Your own build (recommended — an installed one is often behind the pdl)
EMBIODY_LIVE_TEST=1 \
EMBIODY_EXE_PATH=C:/path/to/embiody.exe \
npm run test:live

# Or point at a config file
EMBIODY_LIVE_TEST=1 EMBIODY_TEST_CONFIG=./browserdo.config.yaml npm run test:live
```

Without `EMBIODY_LIVE_TEST=1` the whole group is skipped, so no browser is started by accident.

A custom `EMBIODY_EXE_PATH` automatically gets its own profile derived from the exe path, so it
does not fight the installed build over `DevToolsActivePort` and cannot connect to the wrong one.
The tests only work in tabs they opened themselves and close them at the end; tabs that were
already there are left alone.

## Where the pdl is looked for

The contract tests read `embiody_protocol.pdl`, in this order:

1. `EMBIODY_PDL_PATH`
2. the browser checkout next to this repository: `src/chrome/browser/devtools/embiody_protocol.pdl` inside
   `../../embiody`, relative to this repository

When none is found the group **skips** rather than fails — `npm test` should still be green on a
machine with no embiody checkout.

## When writing a new test

- A new browser action → add a reply-reading case to `module/browser-actions.test.ts`, a row to
  the mapping table in `module/runtime-executor.test.ts` (an assertion there checks the action
  table is fully covered, so a missing row goes red), and a call in `exerciseEveryAction` in
  `contract/protocol-contract.test.ts`.
- A change to how the main loop is orchestrated → `integration/runtime-loop.test.ts`.
- Code that really waits (`browserWait` and the like) → use `t.mock.timers`; do not let the test
  actually sleep. Learned the hard way: the `browserWait` clamp test slept for a real 10 seconds
  and took one file from 0.2s to 10.3s.
- **After fixing a bug, back the fix out again and confirm the new test really goes red.**
  Learned twice: one assertion was written as `indexOf(...) < length`, which is always true and
  can never fail; and a test for "currentUrl is stale after switching tabs" picked the wrong side
  — it used the tab whose old url was a real address, and that tab gets captured anyway, so
  nothing was being tested. Backing the fix out is the only way to find a test that is not
  testing anything.
- **Anything that waits must be configurable, never hard-coded.** Learned three times: the
  `browserWait` clamp test sleeping 10 real seconds, a hard-coded 2-second snapshot retry, and a
  hard-coded 1-second pause between rounds. By the third, integration had grown to 21 seconds.
  Moving them into `wait.*` / `snapshot.*` and setting them to 1ms in the tests brought it back
  to 3.1 seconds. Before adding a sleep, ask how a test will make it fast.
- **When probing real browser behaviour, check the probe's own premises first.** I once reported,
  from an unreliable script, that clicking after an in-document DOM replacement gives a false
  success, and raised a requirement on that basis. That script triggered the replacement with
  `Runtime.evaluate`, and **whether the replacement happened in the tab under test was never
  verified**; with the page replacing itself on a timer and only `browserGetWindowInfo` reading
  the state, all 5 runs failed hard and correctly. The conclusion was the opposite.
- **Do not verify the state under test by a means that changes it.** The second mistake on the
  same problem: to confirm the DOM had really changed I took another snapshot — which is exactly
  what voids the old `snapshotId`, so what got measured was "a second snapshot was taken", not
  "the DOM changed". Judge through a channel that does not disturb the subject (here, the title
  from `browserGetWindowInfo`).
- `test/fixtures/stale-emsn-repro.html` exists for measurements like that: the page replaces its
  own DOM on a timer, so no CDP evaluation is needed and there is no doubt about which tab was
  hit.

# BrowserDo plugin for Claude

[![Listed on mcpservers.org](https://mcpservers.org/badge.svg)](https://mcpservers.org/servers/zhaijunlong/browserdo)

![BrowserDo demo: Claude Code shops in Embiody, keeps going while minimized, and fills a checkout in one combo](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhaijunlong/browserdo/main/assets/browserdo-demo.gif)

[Embiody](https://embiody.com) is a Windows browser your AI agent works in, in the background,
while you keep using your PC and can step in at any time. This plugin connects Claude to it, so
Claude can search, read pages, click, type and fill in forms, including on sites you are signed
in to.

## What is inside

- **The BrowserDo MCP server** ([source](https://github.com/zhaijunlong/browserdo)), started with
  `npx -y browserdo-mcp@0.9.6` from the npm package
  [`browserdo-mcp`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/browserdo-mcp).
- **The `browserdo` skill**, which tells Claude how to use the browser tools well: snapshot the
  page first and act by element number, batch several steps in one call, read pages with BrowserDo
  instead of a fetch tool, search from the search engine's home page, leave sign-in, captchas
  and payment to you, and work in its own tabs.

## Where it works

| | MCP server (the browser tools) | Skill |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code (terminal, IDE extensions, the desktop app's Code tab) | Yes | Yes |
| Cowork in the Claude desktop app | Only when the Cowork session runs on your computer | Yes |
| Chat (claude.ai, the desktop app's Chat, mobile) | No | Yes; it helps only where the BrowserDo desktop extension provides the tools (below) |

Claude runs local MCP servers from plugins only in Claude Code and in local Cowork sessions. To use
BrowserDo in the desktop app's Chat, install the Claude Desktop extension
(`browserdo-mcp-cldd-<version>.mcpb`) from the
[GitHub releases](https://github.com/zhaijunlong/browserdo/releases) instead.

## Requirements

- Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit.
- Node.js 20 or newer (`node -v`). Install it with `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS`.
- The Embiody browser: installed automatically the first time BrowserDo starts (about 140 MB, a
  few minutes). Until it is ready, each tool replies with the progress.

## What it runs, sends and stores

- **npm**: `npx` fetches the `browserdo-mcp` package from the npm registry to start it.
- **First start**: if Embiody is not installed, BrowserDo downloads the Embiody installer from
  GitHub (or a mirror if GitHub can't be reached) and installs it for your Windows user, without
  administrator rights. The installer carries the digital signature of SELECTIOUS PTY LTD, which
  BrowserDo verifies before running it.
- **Browser updates**: the Embiody browser updates itself, checking the signature of every update.
- **No telemetry**: BrowserDo sends no usage statistics or error reports. The browser tools return
  pages only to Claude.
- **Your browser**: Claude works in your own Embiody, in its Default profile, so it can use the
  sites you are signed in to there. Other browsers such as Chrome or Edge are not touched.
- **Log**: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Embiody\BrowserDo\logs` records the URLs visited and the steps taken,
  never page content. At most three 5 MB files.

See the [BrowserDo README](https://github.com/zhaijunlong/browserdo#readme) for the full tool list
and settings, the [privacy policy](https://embiody.com/privacy) and the
[Embiody end-user license agreement](https://embiody.com/eula).

## License

Apache License 2.0. The Embiody browser it installs is covered by the
[Embiody EULA](https://embiody.com/eula).

# Installing BrowserDo (for AI agents)

You are adding BrowserDo, an MCP server, to the client you are running in. It is published on npm
as `browserdo-mcp` and runs through `npx`.

## Do

1. Check the requirements: Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit, and Node.js 20 or newer (`node -v`).
   If Node.js is missing or older, ask the user to run `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS` and restart
   the client, then continue.
2. Add one local (stdio) MCP server to **your own** MCP settings, with command `npx` and arguments
   `-y browserdo-mcp`:

   ```json
   {
     "mcpServers": {
       "browserdo": {
         "command": "npx",
         "args": ["-y", "browserdo-mcp"]
       }
     }
   }
   ```

   No API key or environment variable is needed.
3. Once the server is connected, call `browser_status`. On first use BrowserDo downloads and installs
   the Embiody browser by itself (about 140 MB, a few minutes). Until it is ready, `browser_status`
   and every other tool reply with the progress; call `browser_status` again every half minute or so.
4. When it says the browser is ready or installed, verify with `browser_read_pages` on one page,
   for example `{"urls": ["https://example.com/"]}`. Reading its title means the setup is done.

## Do not

- Never stop or kill node processes (no Stop-Process, taskkill or pkill on node): other programs on
  this computer use them.
- Do not change the MCP settings of other clients (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code and
  so on). The README lists them for their own users.
- Do not clone the repository or build it: the npm package is all that is needed.
- Do not install the browser yourself or look in its folders to see whether it is installed.
  `browser_status` tells you.

## If you are Cline

Cline 4 reads `%USERPROFILE%\.cline\data\settings\cline_mcp_settings.json`. If that folder exists,
edit that file, not the older one under
`%APPDATA%\Code\User\globalStorage\saoudrizwan.claude-dev\settings`. A person can open the same file
from MCP Servers → Edit configuration.

Running `npx -y browserdo-mcp` in a terminal does not install it for you; only the config entry
does. Don't install the package with `npm -g`.

## If something fails

If installing the browser fails, `browser_status` says why and gives a download link the user can
install from by hand; BrowserDo picks it up on the next call.

# Which Embiody each BrowserDo needs

Each BrowserDo release works with one Embiody version and everything newer. The minimum is
`MIN_EMBIODY_VERSION` in `src/browser_version.ts`; raise it, and add a row here, when BrowserDo
starts relying on something only a newer browser has.

| BrowserDo | Oldest Embiody |
| --- | --- |
| 0.9.0 | 0.9.0.3 |

## What happens with an older browser

BrowserDo reads the browser's version from `/json/version` (`Chrome/156.0.8078.12 Embiody/0.9.0.3`)
each time it connects. If it is older than the minimum, every tool call fails with an error that
names both versions. The first one also opens `chrome://settings/help` in the browser, where the
update is fetched. After updating, restart the browser and then the BrowserDo MCP server.

If the version cannot be read at all, for example because the browser is not Embiody, every tool
call fails with an error saying so, and no page is opened.
